idiom_name: protocol requirements + protocol extension defaults, with Self and constrained generics
implementation_notes: Swift expresses CRTP's mixin half directly: a protocol declares the primitive requirements and a protocol extension provides default implementations, so conforming types supply only the primitive - the same division of labour as a CRTP base plus hook. Compile-time polymorphism comes from using the protocol as a generic constraint, where the concrete type is known and the witness can be specialized and inlined; using the protocol as a type (any P, a boxed protocol type) erases the concrete type, and members whose signatures mention Self or Self-rooted associated types are documented as unavailable through the protocol type. The classic CRTP structure (base parameterized on the derived class) has no Swift counterpart and is unnecessary: inside the protocol, Self already is the derived type.
pitfalls: A protocol extension method that is not a protocol requirement is statically dispatched: if a conforming type declares its own greater, generic code constrained on the protocol can still call the extension's version instead of the type's, which is a classic silent-behaviour trap.

Members that mention Self or a Self-rooted associated type (notably == from Equatable) cannot be called on an existential such as any Comparable; constrained generics or an opaque type are required instead.

Retroactive conformance - adding a protocol conformance in an extension of a type you do not own - can collide with another module doing the same, and the compiler treats it as a warning or error rather than choosing one.
